job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Uma Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up before dawn for prayer, then I take two buses to the head office of a company that runs care homes. I'm a payroll assistant. I studied accounting and started in October. I process timesheets for about four hundred carers, fix mistakes and answer their questions, which is the part I like. I share a flat with my cousin Sana, who works in a pharmacy, and in the evening I cook, call my parents and study for my accounting exams.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, nothing dramatic. People will still need paying on time, and carers still call when something is wrong. I'd tell my family that this is a job that's always needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly settled, but money worries me. My loan takes a big bite and the care sector doesn't pay well, even in the office. I have one week of costs saved. If a payment mix-up happened and I was blamed, I'd have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue, learn the payroll system inside out and complete my first accounting exam. I use an AI helper now and then to word difficult emails to carers, and I'd keep doing that carefully. I'd save 40 a month and try not to spend on anything I could do without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady. A bit stretched, but not frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a payment mix-up could be blamed on you. Has that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, in my second week. A carer was paid 120 too little because of a form I'd put in the wrong box. I stayed late to fix it and called her myself to apologise. She said thank you, and that mattered to me more than the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your parents about money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine. They have a small shop and they can't help with my loan, so I don't want them to worry. They'd lend me their last coin, though, and I know that. It makes me work harder.

say: Payroll will always be needed, because carers still call when something is **wrong**.
It's a job that is **always needed**.
think: The loan takes a big bite and I have only **one week** of costs saved.
If a payroll mix-up were blamed on me, I'd have **nowhere to go**.
do: Learn the payroll system **inside out** and pass my first accounting exam.
Save **40 a month**, and use the AI helper carefully for hard emails.
S0.quote: A carer was paid 120 too little because of a form I'd put in the wrong box.
fieldNote: Her pride is **personal service** to carers, tied to her community values.
Hides her **money worries** from parents who have a small shop.
Uses AI in small, careful doses, as a **steady** adopter.

steps.text: Pass the first accounting exam in the spring
Save 40 a month beside the loan payment
Use the AI helper to word careful emails to carers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change payroll, because a lot of it is repeating. But carers will still want a person when something goes wrong. I'd tell colleagues to learn it and be the one who can explain it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the timesheet processing I do is the exact thing software handles. If the company buys a system that reads timesheets and flags errors, the team of five could be two. I started last, so I'd be the first to go, whatever my manager says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new system the minute it's tested and trusted by other teams. I'd ask to move into the carers' helpline side, which needs a person who can listen. I'd keep studying for accounting and add a short course in employment law. And I'd tell Sana, so we could plan the rent together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with some pride, because I'm the one carers phone. That has to count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the helpline would be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the calls are about people's lives: a night shift that wasn't paid or a sick child. A system can't hear that someone is crying. I think the company would still want a human there, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the company disagrees?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to another care firm, or to the council's finance team. I'd also ask my imam whether anyone in our community has contacts. People look after each other where I come from, and I've never been shy of asking.

say: Payroll is mostly repetition, but carers still want a **person** when it goes wrong.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the system and be able to **explain it**.
think: Timesheet processing is what software handles, so a team of five could become **two**.
I started last, so I'd be **first to go**.
do: Learn the system once **other teams** trust it, and ask to join the carers' helpline.
Study **employment law** and warn Sana so we can plan the rent.
feel: **Anxious**, with pride, since I'm the one carers phone.
S1.quote: A system can't hear that someone is crying.
fieldNote: Her stand is a **human touch**: listening to carers in distress.
Turns to **community** contacts and the imam for job leads.
Steady adopter: waits until **others** trust the system, then moves.

steps.text: Learn the new payroll system once other teams trust it
Take a short employment law course on weekends
Ask to move to the carers' helpline team
Ask my imam if anyone knows of finance openings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for families to plan, and we should look after those who lose their work. In my community we help each other, and I'd say we have to do that on a bigger scale. I'd also say it's a test of whether people are looked after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm afraid. In two years I'd have paid about a fifth of my loan and I'd be the junior payroll clerk. The company would have no reason to keep me. I'd have a pass degree and no big skills. It would hit me and Sana, because I'm paying half of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost I could and I'd move in with my parents above their shop, saving the rent. I'd help in the shop and look for any work, even part-time at a care home. I'd stay close to our mosque, where people share food and leads. I'd also apply for any government help I'm entitled to, even though I'd feel awkward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Not shaking, but a lump of worry that doesn't leave. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd feel awkward asking for government help. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was brought up to work for what you have. It's hard to hold out your hand. But I'd do it before I let my parents take on my debt. If a machine took the work, it's not laziness, and I'd tell myself that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain it to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, it's not me, it's the whole world changing, and we are all in it together. My father would nod and say nothing for a long time. Then he'd say, you'll always have a bed here.

say: It's too fast for families, and we must look after those who **lose their work**.
In my community we help each other, and it needs to happen on a **bigger scale**.
think: I'd have repaid about a **fifth** of my loan, and the company would have no reason to keep me.
It would hit **Sana** (my cousin) too, because I pay half the rent.
do: Move in with my parents above their shop, **saving the rent**.
Look for any work, **ask for government help**, and stay close to our mosque.
feel: **Scared**, a lump of worry that doesn't leave.
S2.quote: I was brought up to work for what you have. It's hard to hold out your hand.
fieldNote: Pride in **working** for what you have makes asking for help hard.
Family and mosque are her **first safety net**.
Expects to lose her job and has little cushion, so **alarmed**.

steps.text: Move in above my parents' shop to save the rent
Apply for any government help I'm entitled to
Look for part-time care home work in the evenings
Cut spending to loan payments, food and travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time, and we should use it well. I'd tell people to keep their faith, look after family and learn something that needs a person. I'd say it quietly, at gatherings, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm cautious. By 27 I could have a qualification, a small flat and be on the way to marriage. Or I could be a clerk whose job is gone. It depends on whether I act in the first two years. I tend to wait to see how things go, and that might not be enough here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my accounting qualification and move towards something with people in it, like the helpline or a finance advisor role at the care firm. I'd pay 80 a month on the loan and save 50. I'd learn the AI tools that the company adopts, because I'll need them anyway. And I'd talk to my parents about whether to marry sooner, since a joint income would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little hopeful. It's like the long wait before an exam, but I know I can revise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said marriage sooner. How does that fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my family, it's expected anyway, and my parents have someone in mind. I'd want a partner who shares the work, and who's kind. Two incomes, or two people helping each other, is safer than one. It's not romantic, but it's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be different in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want my parents' shop to still be open. Both of them work six days a week. If online shopping crushes it, I'd have to support them. That's the part I fear more than my own job.

say: Five years gives us time, so keep your **faith**, look after family and learn work that needs a person.
I'd say it **quietly**, at gatherings, not online.
think: By 27 I could have a qualification and a flat, or be a clerk whose job is **gone**.
I tend to **wait and see**, which might not be enough.
do: Finish my **accounting qualification** and move towards the helpline or an advisor role.
Pay **80 a month** on the loan, save 50 and learn the company's AI tools.
feel: A little **hopeful**, like the long wait before an exam when I can still revise.
S3.quote: Two incomes, or two people helping each other, is safer than one. It's not romantic, but it's honest.
fieldNote: Treats **marriage and family** as practical security as well as tradition.
Fears more for her **parents' shop** than her own job.
Admits her **waiting habit**, so mood stays anxious.

steps.text: Finish the accounting qualification by next summer
Apply for the helpline or advisor roles at the care firm
Pay 80 a month on the loan and save 50
Talk to my parents about marrying sooner for a joint income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing. I'd say that families should plan, learn and put money aside. I'd also tell the older generation that their children will need help with the change, and the community has to make sure nobody's left out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly calm. At 32 I could be a qualified accountant, married, with a flat, and have paid off most of the loan. My worry is that I stay too comfortable, and ten years pass without much change. But I know I'm good at steady effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my qualifications in the first three years, and I'd move into an advisory job in the care sector or a small firm. I'd save for a deposit and pay down the loan, and I'd help my parents modernise the shop with simple online ordering. I'd also learn each AI tool once it's proven, so I'd always be one step behind the first users, and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the only one where I imagine hosting my own family for Eid in my own home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your parents' shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up a simple website and a delivery option, with Sana's help. They'd say no at first. They don't like change either. But if I did it for them, slowly, they'd come round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the community stops talking about it and then it all arrives at once. I'd help set up a small group at the mosque to share what we know about work and money. Even a monthly tea would help.

say: Ten years is a **blessing**, so families should plan and put money aside.
The community must make sure **nobody's left out**.
think: At 32 I could be a qualified accountant, **married with a flat**, and nearly debt-free.
My worry is staying too **comfortable** while ten years pass.
do: Finish my **qualifications** in three years and move into advisory work.
Save a **deposit** and help my parents set up online ordering for the shop.
feel: **Calm**, picturing a home where I host my own family.
S4.quote: I imagine hosting my own family for Eid in my own home.
fieldNote: Plans a **community group** at the mosque as part of her answer.
Wants to help her parents **modernise** the shop gently.
Mood is uneasy because income looks safe but the **community** may not be ready.

steps.text: Qualify as an accountant and move into advisory work by 2029
Save a flat deposit and pay down the loan
Set up simple online ordering for my parents' shop with Sana
Start a monthly work-and-money tea at the mosque

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to prepare, and my family would have to carry me. What would help is quick help from the government that doesn't shame people, training that comes with a wage, and my community staying close. I'd also like honest warnings from employers instead of surprises.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of work. I'm afraid of letting my family down. If someone helps me, I'll help somebody else, as soon as I can. That's how I was raised.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of work. I'm afraid of letting my family down.
portrait: Uma is a **22-year-old** payroll assistant at a care-home company, sharing a flat with her cousin Sana.
She is traditional, rooted in family and her mosque, and proud of **serving** the carers she pays.
She uses AI now and then, adopts tools **once others trust them**, and tends to wait and see.
Her first safety net is **family and community**, though she dislikes asking the state for help.
Her mood goes from anxious to **alarmed** in the two-year case, then to uneasy with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there'd be no time to prepare and her family would have to carry her.
whatWouldHelp: **Quick, dignified** government help, training that comes with a wage, and honest warnings from employers.
